title: Data Mapper Pattern
oneLiner: Moves data between in-memory domain objects and a database while keeping the domain model completely unaware persistence exists.

hero.name: The Courier
hero.catchphrase: Your objects never touch the database. I carry data between them.
hero.power: Transfers data between domain objects and the database, keeping the domain model entirely ignorant of SQL, tables, or persistence details.
hero.weakness: Adds a real layer of mapping code — overkill for simple CRUD apps that would be perfectly fine with an ORM's simpler active-record style.
hero.origin: The Courier appeared after a `User` domain class had `save()`, `find()`, and raw SQL strings baked directly into it, making it impossible to unit test business logic without spinning up a real database.

story.problem: The `User` domain class has `save()` and `find()` methods full of raw SQL baked directly into it. Testing `User`'s business logic requires a real database connection, even for logic that has nothing to do with persistence.
story.solution: The Courier introduces a separate `UserMapper` class that knows how to read and write `User` objects to the database. `User` itself has zero knowledge that a database exists.
story.result: User's business logic can be tested with plain in-memory objects, no database required. All persistence knowledge lives entirely inside UserMapper.

before: Domain objects contain raw SQL and persistence logic
Testing business logic requires a real database
Domain model and database schema are tightly coupled
after: Domain objects have zero knowledge of persistence
Business logic tests run with plain in-memory objects
Domain model and database schema can evolve independently

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A unit test for User.calculateLoyaltyTier() fails because it can't connect to a test database it doesn't even need.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I'm testing loyalty tier math, and it's failing because User.save() tries to open a database connection I never asked for.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Courier appears holding a delivery crate, ready to carry data between the domain and the database.
panels.speaker: The Courier
panels.dialogue: Your User object shouldn't know a database exists. Let me carry the data back and forth instead — User just stays pure business logic.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: UserMapper.save(user) and UserMapper.find(id) hold all the SQL. User itself has no save() or find() methods at all.
panels.speaker: The Courier
panels.dialogue: All the persistence knowledge lives in me. User is just data and business rules — nothing about tables, columns, or SQL.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The loyalty-tier test now runs instantly, with a plain in-memory User object, no database in sight.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The test runs in milliseconds now, no database needed at all. User is finally just business logic.

useWhen: You want domain objects to contain pure business logic, fully testable without a database.
The domain model's shape and the database schema need to evolve somewhat independently.
The application's persistence needs are complex enough that a simple active-record ORM style becomes limiting.
avoidWhen: The app is simple CRUD with a domain model that maps almost 1:1 to database tables — an active-record ORM is far less code for the same result.
The team is small and the added mapper layer isn't paying for itself in testability or flexibility.
Performance-critical paths need tightly optimized, hand-tuned queries where a generic mapping layer would add overhead.
commonMistakes: Introducing Data Mapper for a simple app where an active-record ORM (like most default Rails/Django/Laravel setups) would be simpler and just as effective.
Letting persistence details leak back into the domain model anyway (e.g. via database-specific ID types), quietly defeating the separation.
Not testing mappers against a real (or realistic) database, since their entire job is faithfully handling database specifics.

Confusing Data Mapper with Repository — Data Mapper handles low-level object-to-row translation; Repository provides a higher-level, collection-like interface often built on top of one or more mappers.
explanation.realWorldExample: Hibernate/JPA in Java, Doctrine in PHP, and TypeORM's 'Data Mapper mode' (as opposed to its Active Record mode) are real-world Data Mapper implementations, deliberately keeping domain objects free of persistence code.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this different from just using an ORM?

conversation.speaker: The Courier
conversation.message: Many ORMs default to 'Active Record' — the domain object itself has save()/find() baked in. I'm the opposite philosophy: the domain object knows NOTHING about persistence. A separate mapper carries data between the two worlds.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: When is that separation not worth it?

conversation.speaker: The Courier
conversation.message: Simple CRUD apps, honestly. If your domain objects map cleanly to tables and testability against a database isn't a real pain point, Active Record's simplicity usually wins.

codeBattle.scenario: Your domain layer has complex business rules that need thorough unit testing, but every test currently requires spinning up a real database because domain objects have SQL queries baked directly into their methods.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Courier moves all SQL out of the domain objects and into dedicated mapper classes, letting business logic be tested with plain in-memory objects and no database.

quiz.question: What does Data Mapper keep the domain model free of?
options: Any knowledge of the database or persistence mechanism
quiz.answer: Any knowledge of the database or persistence mechanism
quiz.explanation: The domain object stays pure business logic; a separate mapper handles everything about talking to the database.

quiz.question: What is the main testability benefit of Data Mapper?
options: Business logic in domain objects can be unit tested with plain in-memory objects, no database required
It makes every test run against a live production database
It removes the need for any tests at all
quiz.answer: Business logic in domain objects can be unit tested with plain in-memory objects, no database required
quiz.explanation: Because domain objects have no persistence code, testing them requires no database connection at all.

quiz.question: When is Data Mapper likely overkill?
options: For simple CRUD apps where domain objects map almost 1:1 to database tables
For applications with complex business logic needing thorough unit testing
For domain models that need to evolve independently of the database schema
For teams with heavy testing requirements
quiz.answer: For simple CRUD apps where domain objects map almost 1:1 to database tables
quiz.explanation: An active-record ORM is usually simpler and just as effective when the mapping is straightforward.

quiz.question: How does Data Mapper differ from Repository?
options: Data Mapper handles low-level object-to-row translation; Repository provides a higher-level, collection-like interface often built atop mappers
They are the exact same pattern with different names
Repository requires SQL; Data Mapper forbids it
Data Mapper can only be used with NoSQL databases
quiz.answer: Data Mapper handles low-level object-to-row translation; Repository provides a higher-level, collection-like interface often built atop mappers
quiz.explanation: The two patterns are often layered together: Repository as the friendly interface, Data Mapper doing the underlying translation work.
